opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the most interesting shifts happening right now. The traditional picture was pretty clean: pre-training is where the model soaks up broad knowledge from massive amounts of text, and post-training is where you shape behavior. You teach it to follow instructions, be helpful, be safe, and maybe format answers nicely. Post-training was almost seen as the finishing layer.

With agentic AI, that line gets a lot blurrier. When you want a model to plan over many steps, call tools, recover from errors, and keep track of state over a long horizon, those aren't just surface behaviors you can bolt on at the end. They depend on capabilities that have to be there in the base model: long-context reasoning, a sense of cause and effect, an understanding of code and environments. So people are thinking much harder about what goes into pre-training. That means more code, more interaction-like and trajectory-like data, more data that looks like reasoning traces rather than just finished documents.

At the same time, post-training has become much heavier than it used to be. Reinforcement learning in particular is now a substantial compute investment in its own right, not a small fine-tuning pass. You put the model in environments, let it act, and reward it for actually completing tasks. That's a very different signal from imitating human-written text. The model learns from its own experience, which is closer to how you'd want an agent to learn.

So the way I'd frame it is that the two phases are becoming much more co-designed. You can't think of pre-training as "make it smart" and post-training as "make it polite." You have to ask what the base model needs so that RL on agentic tasks is efficient and stable, and what you're going to get from RL that you couldn't get from pre-training. There's also a real question about where the compute should go. The ratio of pre-training to post-training compute is shifting, and I don't think the field has settled on the right balance yet.

The other piece is evaluation. For agents, the thing you care about is end-to-end task success in messy, realistic settings. That feedback increasingly flows back into decisions about pre-training data and architecture, not just post-training recipes. So rather than a pipeline where one stage hands off to the next, it's becoming more of a loop. I think that's the right way to build these systems going forward.

r001.rationale: It says pre-training and post-training are becoming much more co-designed, with evaluation feeding back into a loop rather than a one-way pipeline.

r002.rationale: It says agentic capabilities such as long-context reasoning must be present in the base model and cannot simply be bolted on during post-training.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's one I think about a lot, because when I was working on PaLM the mental model was pretty clean. Pre-training was where you built the capability, and post-training was this relatively thin layer on top. You'd do some instruction tuning, some RLHF, and the job of that layer was mostly to shape the behavior, make the model helpful and safe, make it follow the format you wanted. The capability itself was baked in by scale.

I think agents really blur that line, and in a few ways.

The first is just the nature of the data. Pre-training data is a snapshot of the world as humans wrote it down. It's text, it's code, it's documents. But what an agent needs to learn is how to act over many steps, how to call a tool, look at the result, recover when the result is wrong, and keep going toward a goal. That kind of trajectory data barely exists on the internet. Nobody writes down the forty dead ends they hit before the thing worked. So increasingly that signal has to be generated, either synthetically or through the model interacting with environments, and that pushes a lot of the real learning into what we used to call post-training. It's not a thin layer anymore. In some labs the compute going into RL and agentic fine-tuning is becoming comparable to pre-training.

The second shift is in what you're optimizing. In pre-training you're optimizing next-token prediction, which is a very local objective. For an agent you care about the outcome of a long horizon. Did the task actually get done? Did the code pass the tests? Did the research question get answered? That's a reward that only shows up at the end, and reinforcement learning is really the natural tool for it. So you get this interesting situation where the long-horizon objectives are now being fed back into the pre-training mix, with people folding agentic trajectories and tool-use data into the base corpus itself, because they've realized that if the base model has never seen a tool call, you're fighting an uphill battle later.

And the third thing, which I think is underappreciated, is evaluation. In the old regime you could evaluate the pre-trained model on perplexity and a handful of benchmarks and have a decent sense of what you had. With agents, the base model's quality is almost unobservable until you put it in a loop with tools and an environment. So the feedback cycle between the two stages gets much tighter. You learn something about what the agent can't do, and that informs what you put in the next pre-training run.

So if I had to summarize, I'd say we're moving from two sequential phases toward something more like a continuum, where pre-training gives you broad priors about the world and post-training teaches the model how to use those priors to act. The boundary is still there organizationally, because the compute regimes are different and the teams are different, but conceptually it's getting a lot blurrier, and I think that's healthy.

r001.rationale: The response describes pre-training and post-training as moving from sequential phases toward a continuum, with a blurrier boundary and feedback between them.

r002.rationale: It discusses adding agentic trajectories and tool-use data to pre-training, but does not ask whether reasoning capabilities should be developed there rather than introduced during post-training.

astra-6.text:
I think agentic AI makes the relationship between pre-training and post-training much more iterative. Pre-training gives you the foundation: knowledge, representations, and the ability to generalize. But an agent has to use those capabilities over multiple steps. It needs to decide when to call a tool, interpret the result, and change course if something doesn’t work. That puts more emphasis on post-training and on learning from interactions.

The interesting question is where the learning signal comes from. For a single response, you might be able to judge its quality directly. For an agent, an individual step can look reasonable, but the overall task can still fail. So you need to evaluate the trajectory and the outcome, and then figure out which decisions contributed to that outcome.

I wouldn’t say that makes pre-training less important. A stronger foundation can make those behaviors easier to learn. But I expect a tighter feedback loop, where what we learn from training and evaluating agents also informs what capabilities we want to build during pre-training.

r001.rationale: The response describes a more iterative relationship and feedback loop between pre-training and post-training, but does not clearly propose unifying them.

r002.rationale: The response does not ask whether reasoning capabilities should be developed during pre-training rather than introduced only during post-training.

sol-6.1.text:
I think agentic AI makes that boundary more fluid. Pre-training gives you a strong foundation: the knowledge, the representations, and some of the reasoning capabilities. But an agent has to do more than generate a good answer. It has to take an action, observe what happened, and decide what to do next. That makes post-training increasingly important, because you’re training for success over a sequence of decisions.

And the feedback becomes interesting. Did the agent actually complete the task? Did it use the right tools? Could it recover when something went wrong? Those are different signals from predicting the next token, and getting reliable signals over long tasks is a real challenge.

I wouldn’t say that means pre-training becomes less important. You still need a capable base model to generalize to unfamiliar situations. The question is how to allocate compute and data across those stages, and how the experience you collect from agents can feed back into the next round of training. I see it becoming more of an iterative loop.

r001.rationale: The response describes the boundary as more fluid and says agent experience can feed back into another round of training, framing the stages as an iterative loop.

r002.rationale: It says pre-training provides some reasoning capabilities, but does not ask whether reasoning should be developed there rather than introduced only during post-training.
